title: Many years to God
hookLine: God appears in the sky over a city, and the old devotee's first worry is that someone might put the evil eye on him
carry: vatsalya: loving god like your own child
tomorrow: ten verses say they're part of a thousand. where's the rest?

lines: A WORD AGAINST THE EVIL EYE.
THE OLD MAN WORRIES FOR HIM.
cards: A grandmother sees a beautiful baby in the street and, before anything else, says a quick word against the evil eye. Too much praise, the old worry goes, and something bad might follow. Now move that instinct.

The Sri Vaishnava tradition tells of a temple garland-maker named Vishnuchitta who, on a day of great honor, looked up and saw Vishnu himself in the sky, riding the eagle Garuda, come to watch. Crowds everywhere.
The old man's first feeling wasn't awe, or a request. It was worry: someone might cast the evil eye on him. So he did what that grandmother does.
He sang a blessing over God.

teach.b: The blessing is the Tiruppallandu, and its key word is pallandu, many years. Many years, many years, the song begins, to your holy feet.
Then the blessing spreads: many years to the goddess at your side, to the wheel and to the conch.
It's what you sing over a child or an elder you love, and here it's sung to the Lord of the universe. Tradition says that's why Vishnuchitta came to be called Periyalvar, the great Alvar.
Tradition says he also found and raised Andal, whose dawn vow came two days ago, so a father and a daughter both sit among the Alvars. His longer hymns keep the same tenderness.

In them he sings as Yashoda, Krishna's foster mother: rocking the cradle, coaxing the toddler to come for his bath, calling the moon down to play with him. God as a little one who needs looking after.

Hindu teachers have a word for this kind of love: vatsalya, a parent's love, given back to God. It's why many Hindu homes care for a small image of baby Krishna: bathing him, feeding him, singing him to sleep.
A prayer can bring God a need. Periyalvar brings God his care. Love, in these hymns, isn't only being protected; it's wanting to protect.

how: Sri Vaishnavas sing Periyalvar's Tiruppallandu in their temples and homes as a blessing over the Lord, alongside Periyalvar's songs of Yashoda and the child Krishna.

o: Sanskrit verses recited by priests at sunrise
Tamil songs of devotion to Vishnu by poet-saints
folk tunes sung in the fields at harvest time

p: a parent's love, given to God

s: when Vishnu appeared, Periyalvar asked him for a blessing
he did the opposite: he sang a blessing over Vishnu, many years.
Periyalvar sings some hymns as Krishna's foster mother
as Yashoda: cradle songs, bath time, the moon called down to play.
so a father and a daughter both sit among the Alvars.

games.q: you're Vishnuchitta. after a day of great honor, you look up and see Vishnu in the sky, in front of the whole city. what's your first move?
o: ask for something you've always wanted.
sing a blessing over him, against the evil eye.
games.why: tradition says he worried for God and sang pallandu, many years, a blessing Sri Vaishnavas still sing.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love and see them clearly, their face, their hands. Instead of wanting anything from them, wish them long life, many years, many years, letting the wish travel out with each breath.
If another person comes to mind, bless them too; if you pray, let the blessing rise toward the name you pray to, the way Periyalvar did.

wordCard.voice: The Alvar hymns. Today, Periyalvar's many years: a blessing sung over God, and the love of a parent given back to the divine.

orig.note: Tamil: many years, the refrain of Periyalvar's blessing over God, the Tiruppallandu.

carryVoice: Your line: vatsalya, loving God like your own child. Many years, sung over the one who keeps the world. That's today, done.
